t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we learn to detect silver, copper, manganese and chromium cations in the mineralisate. The work is connected with quantitative analysis by the PEC method. The aim is to become familiar with the significance and methods of analysis of the manganese, chromium and silver cations isolated with sulphuric and nitric acids. The cations are detected in the filtrate of the mineralisate.

By the end of the session you should be able to detect from the filtrate the manganese cation that may be present in the mineralisate. In the same way, you will detect the chromium and silver cations in the filtrate. One more outcome: to be able to give an interpretation of each reaction in the book according to the requirements of forensic chemical analysis. That is, besides carrying out the reaction, you are required to explain its result from the forensic chemical point of view.

The following will be needed for the work: mineralisate, filter paper, funnel, reagents, test tubes, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. In the methods, a separatory funnel, water bath, universal indicator and microscope are used. This equipment occurs again and again in the reactions that follow, so remember its names well.

This is the session map. Four cations are detected in the mineralisate: silver, copper, manganese and chromium. For silver, the dithizone reaction, the AgCl precipitate and microcrystalline reactions are carried out. For copper, diethyldithiocarbamate and three portions of qualitative reactions are used. Manganese is detected with periodate and persulphate, producing a violet colour. For chromium, the perchromic acid and diphenylcarbazide reactions are carried out. Remember: manganese interferes with the detection of chromium, and sodium azide is used to eliminate it.

Now the dithizonate reaction of silver. 5 ml of mineralisate is placed in a separatory funnel, 5 ml of chloroform is added, and 0.01% dithizone, as a solution in chloroform, is added dropwise. The mixture is shaken thoroughly. If the silver cation is present, the chloroform layer is coloured yellow-orange. An important point: the mercury cation also forms with dithizone a coloured compound similar to that of silver, so this result alone is not sufficient.

The dithizonates of silver and mercury must be distinguished from each other. For this the chloroform layer is separated, 5 ml of 0.5N HCl is added, and the mixture is shaken. With silver dithizonate the yellow-orange colour changes to blue-green. With mercury dithizonate the colour does not change. If the dithizone reaction does not occur at all, the analysis for silver is stopped. If it does occur, additional reactions are carried out.

We compare manganese and chromium. Manganese is oxidised with potassium periodate or ammonium persulphate, and in both methods a violet colour forms. In the case of chromium, trivalent chromium is oxidised by persulphate to the hexavalent state, after which diphenylcarbazide is added. The table shows: for manganese the result is violet, for chromium red-violet. Remember: in detecting chromium with diphenylcarbazide, manganese interferes.

The stage of separating silver from the other cations. To 90 ml of mineralisate, 0.5 g of table salt is added, and a white turbid silver chloride precipitate forms. The mixture is heated to boiling and filtered. The filtrate is tested for copper, antimony, zinc, arsenic and other cations. The silver chloride precipitate on the filter is dissolved in 2.5 ml of 25% ammonium hydroxide. In this way two lines of work are obtained from one sample.

This slide gives the reaction scheme of the AgCl precipitate. Reagents: 90 ml of mineralisate and 0.5 g of table salt. Condition: heating to boiling and filtration. As product, AgCl forms, that is, a white turbid precipitate. The observation is this: Cu, Sb, Zn and As remain in the filtrate, while the precipitate is dissolved in 2.5 ml of 25% NH4OH. Thus silver passes into the precipitate and the other cations remain in the filtrate.

Three reactions are carried out with the silver solution. The first: a drop of the solution is dried slowly on a microscope slide at room temperature, and under the microscope clear crystals in the shape of cubes, octahedra and quadrilaterals are seen. The second: a saturated solution of thiourea and a drop of potassium picrate are added to the residue, and a cluster of yellow needle-shaped crystals forms. The third: 0.5 ml of saturated potassium iodide solution is added to 0.5 ml of ammoniacal solution, and a yellowish turbidity and precipitate appear.

We summarise the key parameters for silver. In the dithizone reaction, 5 ml of mineralisate, 5 ml of chloroform and a few drops of 0.01% dithizone in chloroform are used. To distinguish mercury and silver dithizonates, 5 ml of 0.5N HCl is taken. For AgCl, 90 ml of mineralisate and 0.5 g of table salt are needed, and the precipitate is dissolved in 2.5 ml of 25% ammonium hydroxide. These figures must be remembered exactly.

Now copper. The diethyldithiocarbamate reaction is carried out for copper. 10 ml of mineralisate is brought to pH 3 with ammonia, using universal indicator. Then 5 ml of a chloroform solution of lead diethyldithiocarbamate is added and the mixture is shaken. If copper is present, the chloroform layer is coloured yellow-brown. If there is no colour, no other tests are carried out for copper.

Purifying the copper extract consists of several stages. First the chloroform layer is separated and washed for 30 seconds with 6N HCl to remove excess lead diethyldithiocarbamate, then with water. Then it is shaken with a 1% solution of mercury(II) chloride until the colour disappears. To the colourless mixture, 0.5-1 ml of water is added and shaken, the aqueous layer is taken off and divided into three portions. A separate qualitative reaction is carried out in each portion.

To confirm copper, reactions are carried out on three portions. With 10 drops of 2% CdCl2 and 5% K4[Fe(CN)6], a pale violet precipitate forms. With 0.2 g ZnSO4 and NH4 tetrathiocyanatomercurate, a pale violet precipitate is also obtained. With pyridine thiocyanate, 1-2 ml of the reagent is added until turbidity appears, then 1 ml of chloroform; the lower layer becomes clear blue. The results are interpreted according to the requirements of forensic chemistry.

The key values for copper. For analysis, 10 ml of mineralisate is taken and brought to pH 3. To it, 5 ml of a chloroform solution of lead diethyldithiocarbamate is added. The chloroform layer is washed for 30 seconds with 6N HCl, then with water. It is shaken with 1% mercury(II) chloride until the colour disappears, and then 0.5-1 ml of water is added. This sequence serves to purify and isolate copper.

Oxidation of manganese with potassium periodate. Into a test tube are placed 1 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of water, 1 ml of saturated monobasic sodium phosphate solution, 1 drop of 10% AgNO3 and 0.2 g of KIO4. The mixture is heated on a water bath for 20 minutes. If manganese is present, the mixture is coloured violet. We assess the result by this colour.

Oxidation of manganese with ammonium persulphate. To 1 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of water and 1 ml of saturated monobasic sodium phosphate solution are added, and the mixture is heated for 5-6 minutes on a water bath. Then to the boiling mixture, 1 drop of 10% silver nitrate and 0.5 g of ammonium persulphate are added. Heating continues until the evolution of gas bubbles stops. If manganese is present, a violet colour forms.

Both reactions of manganese are compared, and it is explained how manganese poisoning is confirmed. In the periodate method, 0.2 g of KIO4 is taken and heated for 20 minutes; in the persulphate method, 0.5 g of (NH4)2S2O8 is used, heated for 5-6 minutes and then continued until the bubbles stop. In both methods the result is violet. The question is this: how is the result assessed if it is positive with periodate and negative with persulphate, and why? Think about this question.

The key parameters for manganese. In the periodate method, 1 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of water, 1 ml of monobasic sodium phosphate, 1 drop of 10% AgNO3 and 0.2 g of potassium periodate are taken. The mixture is heated on a water bath for 20 minutes. In the persulphate method, 0.5 g of ammonium persulphate is used, and heating continues until the evolution of gas bubbles stops. The two methods differ in the reagent, while the preparatory part is similar.

Now chromium, the perchromic acid reaction. To 5 ml of mineralisate, 30% NaOH is added to pH 7, 1 drop of 10% AgNO3 and 0.5 g of persulphate are added, and the mixture is heated on a water bath for 20 minutes. After cooling, 1 ml of monobasic sodium phosphate, 1 ml of ethyl acetate and 2-3 drops of perhydrol are added. If chromium is present, the organic solvent layer is coloured.

Detecting chromium with diphenylcarbazide. First, 1 ml of mineralisate, 4 ml of water, 1 drop of 10% AgNO3 and 0.5 g of ammonium persulphate are heated on a water bath for 20 minutes: Cr(III) is oxidised to Cr(VI), that is, trivalent chromium passes to the hexavalent state. Then 1 ml of monobasic sodium phosphate is added and the pH is brought to 1.7 with 10% KOH. Finally, 1 ml of a 0.25% solution of diphenylcarbazide in ethanol-acetone, 1:1, is added. If chromium is present, a red-violet colour forms.

In detecting chromium, manganese interferes. In such cases, a drop of concentrated H2SO4 and crystals of sodium azide are added to the mineralisate and mixed until the red colour formed disappears. After that, a 1% alcoholic solution of diphenylcarbazide is added. If chromium is present, a pink or red colour forms. That is, we first eliminate the interference, and then detect chromium.

The key values for chromium. In the perchromic method, 5 ml of mineralisate is neutralised with 30% NaOH to pH 7, 0.5 g of persulphate is added and the mixture is heated for 20 minutes. In the diphenylcarbazide method, the pH is brought to 1.7 with 10% KOH and 1 ml of 0.25% reagent is added. If manganese is present, the interference is removed with concentrated H2SO4 and sodium azide. It is important to be able to tell these values apart by method.

We summarise the results. For silver, dithizone is used; for copper, diethyldithiocarbamate; for manganese, periodate or persulphate; for chromium, diphenylcarbazide. Signs: with silver the chloroform is yellow-orange; with copper at pH 3 the chloroform is yellow-brown; with manganese the mixture is violet; with chromium red-violet. The task is set of writing the chemical equation for all the reactions.

The colouring of the organic layer is the main sign of detection. Silver dithizonate gives a yellow-orange colour in the chloroform layer. Copper diethyldithiocarbamate colours the chloroform layer yellow-brown. In detecting chromium as perchromate, ethyl acetate is added as the solvent; if chromium is present, the organic layer is coloured. The table gives the solvent, reagent and result for each cation.

Let us recall step by step the analysis pathway for silver. If there is no reaction with dithizone, the analysis for silver is stopped. If there is, the dithizonate is distinguished from mercury dithizonate with 0.5N HCl: with silver the colour changes to blue-green. Then with 0.5 g of table salt the AgCl precipitate is separated and dissolved in 2.5 ml of 25% NH4OH. In the ammoniacal solution the microcrystalline and KI reactions are carried out.

t: "I know - I want to know - I learned"
n: With this method you assess your own knowledge during the session. A table is completed individually: "I know", "I want to know", "I learned". Topic: detection of silver, copper, manganese and chromium cations in the mineralisate. The method helps to assess the level of knowledge gained, to explore the need to enrich knowledge, and allows the student to express a conclusion of their own. At the end of the session the "Most active group", the "Most knowledgeable group", the "Quickest-witted group" and the "Most knowledgeable student of today's session" are determined.

t: Case 10: yellow-green colour of the mineralisate
n: Now a case. When the object was mineralised, the mineralisate was yellowish-green. The task is this: to determine which metallic poison this colour belongs to, to explain the cause and the solution, and to carry out the forensic chemical analysis. Columns of the answer table: type of problem, causes of origin and ways of resolving it. Build your answer along these three columns.

Situational problem. In the summer season, Sh. Aliyev ate ready-made food and salads. When he vomited, he was given 1 litre of dilute KMnO4 solution and baking soda to drink. Because the poisoning was severe, death occurred, and a diagnosis of heavy metal poisoning was made. Physical evidence in 250 g jars: liver 100 g, kidneys 200 g, portions of stomach and intestine 300 g. In the preliminary analysis the mineralisate gave a yellow colour with dithizone. Question: which metal does this colour belong to?

Review questions of the first block. Why is the reaction for the manganese cation carried out in the presence of monobasic sodium phosphate and silver nitrate? Why is a solution of monobasic sodium phosphate used in detecting the chromium cation with diphenylcarbazide? Which cations interfere with the detection of silver dithizonate, and how can they be separated? What are the conditions for forming the copper diethyldithiocarbamate complex and for its re-extraction? Answer each question on the basis of the reactions covered.

t: Reactions for which equations are written
n: Now the reactions for which equations are written. For silver, chemical equations are written for the dithizonate reaction, for distinguishing mercury and silver dithizonates, and for the AgCl precipitate. For copper, the task is set of writing equations for the formation of diethyldithiocarbamate and for the reactions of the three portions. For manganese and chromium, the equations of the periodate, persulphate, perchromate and diphenylcarbazide reactions are written. The table gives the pages in the book: 202, 203 and 203-204.

The requirement for forensic chemical interpretation is set in three directions. For copper, an interpretation is given according to the requirements of forensic chemical analysis, based on the results of the three-portion reactions. For manganese, both reactions are compared and it is explained in which case manganese poisoning is confirmed. For chromium, the reaction results are interpreted according to the requirements of forensic chemical analysis. That is, it is not enough merely to record the result; it must be explained from the forensic chemical point of view.

Review questions on manganese. Explain, on the basis of chemical equations, the reactions for detecting the manganese cation in the mineralisate. How is the result assessed if it is positive with periodate and negative with persulphate, and why? Why is the manganese reaction carried out in the presence of monobasic sodium phosphate and silver nitrate? By what method is the quantity of the manganese cation determined? Owing to which cation does the mineralisate turn violet when oxidised with potassium periodate?

Review questions on chromium. What are the bases of detecting the chromium cation in the object under examination? What colour does the chromium cation give the mineralisate? Which reactions are taken as the basis in the fractional detection of chromium in a biological object? Why is a solution of monobasic sodium phosphate used in detecting chromium with diphenylcarbazide? How can the quantity of the chromium cation be determined?

Review questions on silver. Explain, on the basis of chemical reactions, the methods of establishing the identity of the silver cation in the mineralisate. Why is the examination for silver carried out after the examination for the chromium and manganese cations? Which microcrystal-forming reactions are used in detecting silver? What are the methods of determining the quantity of silver, and what is the advantage of the colorimetric method over the volumetric method? Which cations interfere with the detection of silver dithizonate, and how can they be separated?

The first part of the review questions on copper. Which reactions are used to establish the identity of the copper cation? Write the conditions for forming the copper diethyldithiocarbamate complex and its chemical equation. Write the conditions for re-extracting copper from the copper diethyldithiocarbamate complex. What are the reactions for testing the eluate for copper, and their chemical equations? Explain the methods and conditions for separating the copper cation from other metal cations.

The second part of the review questions on copper. Indicate, on the basis of reactions, the organic reagents used in separating metal cations and in establishing their identity and quantity. Explain with examples the use of the reagent dithizone in detecting toxicologically significant metal cations. How is the copper cation detected by the fractional method? Write the methods of determining the quantity of copper; show and prove the possibility of determination by the colorimetric method.

On safety and working procedure. The reactions are carried out in a separatory funnel and on a water bath. Heating continues up to the stated time and state: 20 minutes, or until the gas bubbles stop. In the reactions, chloroform, 6N HCl, concentrated H2SO4, mercury(II) chloride and perhydrol are used, so caution is necessary. The results must be checked and properly recorded in the laboratory notebook.
